description_full: Old National Bancorp operates as the bank holding company for Old National Bank that provides consumer and commercial banking services in the United States. It accepts deposit accounts, such as noninterest-bearing demand, interest-bearing checking and negotiable order of withdrawal, savings and money market, and time deposits. The company also offers loans, including home equity lines of credit, residential real estate loans, and consumer loans, as well as loans to commercial clients comprising commercial loans, commercial real estate loans, agricultural loans, letters of credit, and lease financing. In addition, it offers debit and automated teller machine cards, telephone access and online banking, and other electronic and mobile banking services. Further, the company offers private banking, wealth management, trust, investment advisory, brokerage, and foreign currency services; treasury management, merchant, and capital markets services for businesses; and community development lending and equity investment solutions. Old National Bancorp was founded in 1834 and is headquartered in Evansville, Indiana.

Revenue per employee of $516K ranks in the above the sector median among Financial Services peers, improving at 13%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $130K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $8K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 7× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Old National Bancorp is a mid-cap financial services business with a $9.4B market cap on $2.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +16% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 9% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $637M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.02× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 33% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.29x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+13.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 24% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 24% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.49 vs 5y 0.80), so read it loosely.
About $99.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 44% below its DCF fair value of $44.83, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $34.57 to $60.27 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 39% below its 10-year median.
The 15 covering analysts target $28.90 on average, 16% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 1.2% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 8.9%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.51).
It converts 25% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 2.73% and an efficiency ratio of 93% (cost-heavy).
It earns a 8% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 12.1% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.45% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.5% over 3 years, 24.8% over 5 years and 15.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 2.2% on average.
Analysts expect 8.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 88%.
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (0.8% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 18.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 19.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,894 employees, each generates about $516K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 13.3% a year.
That works out to $130K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
